title: Handling Events
summary: **Event handling** in React lets you respond to user actions — clicks, typing, form submits — by attaching functions to JSX props like onClick, onChange, and onSubmit, wrapped in React's cross-browser SyntheticEvent.

subtopics.title: Attaching handlers in JSX
subtopics.explanation: React event props are camelCased (onClick, onChange, onSubmit) and take a function reference, not a string or a function call. Writing onClick={handleClick()} calls the function during render and assigns its return value, which is a classic bug; you want onClick={handleClick} or onClick={() => handleClick(id)}. This is the single most common beginner mistake in event handling.

subtopics.title: SyntheticEvent
subtopics.explanation: React wraps every native DOM event in a SyntheticEvent, a cross-browser normalized object exposing a consistent API like e.target, e.preventDefault(), and e.stopPropagation(). This means your handlers behave the same on Chrome, Safari, and Firefox. You can still reach the raw browser event via e.nativeEvent when you need engine-specific data.

subtopics.title: Event delegation
subtopics.explanation: React does not attach a listener to every element. Instead it attaches a small number of listeners at the root container (the document in React 16, the root node in React 17+) and lets native events bubble up to it. This keeps listener counts tiny so a list of 1,000 rows with onClick costs almost nothing extra at mount time.

subtopics.title: preventDefault
subtopics.explanation: Calling e.preventDefault() inside a handler stops the browser's built-in behavior for that event. The canonical case is a form's onSubmit, where the default is a full-page navigation that would wipe your component state. Forgetting it produces the infamous 'form reloads the page' bug.

subtopics.title: stopPropagation
subtopics.explanation: e.stopPropagation() prevents the event from bubbling up to parent handlers in React's tree. It is essential when a clickable element sits inside another clickable element, such as a Delete button inside a selectable row. Without it, clicking Delete would also trigger the row's onClick select handler.

subtopics.title: Passing arguments to handlers
subtopics.explanation: To pass extra data like an item id to a shared handler, wrap it in an arrow function: onClick={() => handleClick(id)}. The arrow closes over the id so each element gets its own value. An alternative for large lists is one shared handler that reads a data-id attribute from e.target, avoiding a new closure per row.

subtopics.title: Capture vs bubble phase
subtopics.explanation: React supports both event phases. Standard props like onClick fire during the bubble phase (target up to root), while Capture-suffixed props like onClickCapture fire during the capture phase (root down to target). This lets a parent intercept an event before the child handles it, which is useful for things like global click-outside logic.

subtopics.title: Event pooling history
subtopics.explanation: In React 16 and earlier, SyntheticEvents were pooled and reused for performance, so their properties were nulled out after the handler returned. To use an event asynchronously you had to call e.persist(). React 17 removed pooling, so events now behave like ordinary objects and e.persist() is effectively a no-op kept for backward compatibility.

foundations.overview: React event handling lets your UI react to what users do. You attach a function to a JSX prop such as onClick or onChange, and React calls that function with an event object whenever the action happens. It looks like plain HTML event attributes but is camelCased and takes a function reference, not a string.
foundations.formalDefinition: An event handler in React is a function passed to a camelCased event prop (onClick, onChange, onSubmit, etc.) on a JSX element. React invokes the handler with a SyntheticEvent — a normalized wrapper around the native browser event — when the corresponding DOM event fires.
foundations.whyItMatters: Events are the bridge between the user and your application state. Without event handlers a UI is static; with them you can update state, submit forms, and drive every interaction. Interviewers test events because almost every component you ever write will handle at least one.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an event prop as a doorbell button. You hand React a function (the action to run when the bell rings). When the user presses the button, React rings the bell by calling your function and hands it a slip of paper (the event object) describing what happened.
foundations.browserPerspective: React does NOT attach a separate listener to every element. It attaches a few listeners at the root of your app and lets real DOM events bubble up to it — this is event delegation. When an event reaches the root, React figures out which component it targeted, wraps the native event in a SyntheticEvent, and calls the matching handlers in order.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Buttons that submit or save, text inputs that update state on every keystroke, forms that validate and submit, dropdowns that open on click, drag-and-drop, keyboard shortcuts — all of these are built on event handlers.
foundations.businessImpact: Smooth, correct event handling is what makes a product feel responsive. A button that does nothing, a form that reloads the page, or a double-submit that charges a card twice all erode trust and cost revenue.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing how SyntheticEvents, delegation, preventDefault, and stopPropagation work prevents whole categories of bugs — accidental page reloads, events firing twice, handlers receiving the wrong arguments.
foundations.performanceImpact: Because React uses delegation, you rarely pay for thousands of individual listeners. The main cost to watch is creating a brand-new inline arrow function on every render, which can cause memoized children to re-render unnecessarily.
commonUseCases: Click handlers on buttons and links (onClick)
Reading input as the user types (onChange)
Passing extra arguments such as an item id to a shared handler
Stopping a click from bubbling to a parent (stopPropagation)

commonMisconceptions.myth: React attaches a real DOM listener to every element with an onClick.
commonMisconceptions.reality: React uses event delegation — it attaches a small number of listeners at the app root and dispatches events to your handlers from there.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The event object is a normal native browser event.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It is a SyntheticEvent — a cross-browser wrapper. Historically React pooled and reused these objects, so old code that read e.persist() did so to keep the event after the handler returned. Pooling was removed in React 17, so the event now behaves like a normal object.
That CALLS handleClick during render and passes its return value. You must pass a reference (onClick={handleClick}) or an arrow wrapper (onClick={() => handleClick(id)}).

config.intro: React doesn't listen on every node. Here is the path a real click takes from the browser to your function.

steps.name: User clicks
steps.detail: The browser fires a native click event on the target element (e.g., a <button>).

steps.name: Event bubbles
steps.detail: The native event bubbles up the real DOM tree toward the document/root where React listens.

steps.name: React catches it at the root
steps.detail: React's single delegated listener receives the event and identifies which React element was the target.

steps.name: SyntheticEvent is created
steps.detail: React wraps the native event in a normalized SyntheticEvent so behaviour is consistent across browsers.

steps.name: Handlers run in order
steps.detail: React calls your onClick handler (and any parent handlers as it walks up the component tree) with the SyntheticEvent.

steps.name: You control flow
steps.detail: Inside the handler you can call preventDefault() to stop default behaviour or stopPropagation() to stop bubbling to parents.

interactiveExamples.title: onClick, onChange, and onSubmit together
interactiveExamples.explanation: A button uses onClick, the input uses onChange to track typing, and the form uses onSubmit with preventDefault so the page does not reload.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Typing updates state live; submitting shows a greeting without reloading the page; Clear resets both fields.

interactiveExamples.title: Passing arguments and stopping propagation
interactiveExamples.explanation: Each list item shares one handler but passes its own id via an arrow wrapper. Clicking Delete calls stopPropagation so it does not also trigger the row's select handler.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Clicking a row selects it. Clicking Delete logs the id but does NOT select the row, because stopPropagation halts bubbling.

codeLab.title: Wire up a like button
codeLab.instructions: Add state for a like count and an onClick handler that increments it. Show the current count in the button label.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Clicking the button increases the like count shown in its label.
hints: Pass a function reference or arrow function to onClick, not a function call.
Use the functional updater setCount((c) => c + 1) so rapid clicks stay correct.

debuggingLab.title: The form that reloads the page
debuggingLab.symptom: Submitting the form flashes and reloads the whole page, wiping the result.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: A <form> with a submit button triggers the browser's default behaviour: a full-page navigation/reload. React's handler runs, but the page reloads immediately afterward, throwing away your component state and the message you just set.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to accept the event argument and call e.preventDefault() in onSubmit.
Putting the handler on the button's onClick instead of the form's onSubmit, which misses Enter-key submissions.
Calling handleSubmit() (with parentheses) in JSX instead of passing the reference.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Accept the SyntheticEvent and call preventDefault() so the page no longer reloads.

theory.question: What is a SyntheticEvent in React, and why does React use it?
theory.directAnswer: A SyntheticEvent is a lightweight, cross-browser wrapper that React puts around the native DOM event. React passes it to your event handlers so they behave identically across browsers, with a consistent API like e.target, e.preventDefault(), and e.stopPropagation().

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An object that mirrors the native browser event but normalizes differences between browsers and exposes a predictable, standardized interface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Historically browsers implemented events inconsistently. The SyntheticEvent layer gives developers one reliable API and lets React power its delegation system, so you never worry about which browser the user is on.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When a native event reaches React's root listener, React creates a SyntheticEvent wrapping it and dispatches it to your handlers. You can still reach the underlying native event via e.nativeEvent. In React 16 and earlier these objects were pooled and reused for performance, so you had to call e.persist() to use them asynchronously; React 17 removed pooling, so the event behaves like an ordinary object now.

theory.whyImportant: It explains why event behaviour is consistent and is the basis for understanding delegation, preventDefault, and the old event-pooling gotcha — all common interview territory.
theory.realWorldExample: An onChange handler reads e.target.value the same way whether the user is on Chrome, Safari, or Firefox, because the SyntheticEvent normalizes the shape of the event.

nestedTopics.title: Event pooling history
nestedTopics.explanation: Before React 17, SyntheticEvents were pooled (reused) so properties were nulled after the handler ran; you called e.persist() to keep one. Pooling was removed in React 17.

nestedTopics.title: nativeEvent
nestedTopics.explanation: e.nativeEvent gives you the raw underlying browser event when you need browser-specific data.

nestedTopics.title: Cross-browser normalization
nestedTopics.explanation: SyntheticEvent smooths over differences in property names and behaviour across browser engines.

followUps.question: Do you still need e.persist() today?
followUps.answer: No. Since React 17 events are no longer pooled, so you can read the event asynchronously without persisting it. e.persist() still exists but is effectively a no-op for this purpose.

theory.question: How does React attach event listeners under the hood, and what is event delegation?
theory.directAnswer: React does not attach a listener to each element. It attaches a small number of listeners at the root container and relies on native events bubbling up to that root. This is event delegation: one listener handles events for the entire subtree and dispatches them to the right React handlers.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Event delegation is the pattern of listening at a single ancestor instead of on every descendant, then determining the real target when an event bubbles up.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Attaching thousands of listeners is wasteful in memory and setup time. Delegation keeps listener count tiny and makes adding/removing elements cheap, since no per-element listener has to be wired or torn down.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: React 17+ attaches its listeners to the root DOM node you render into (rather than document, as in React 16). When a native event bubbles to that root, React reconstructs the component path and calls handlers from target up to root, simulating capture and bubble phases on its SyntheticEvents.

theory.whyImportant: It explains React's performance characteristics and why stopPropagation behaves the way it does — interviewers love to probe whether you understand delegation versus per-node listeners.
theory.realWorldExample: A list with 1,000 rows each having an onClick costs almost nothing extra, because there is still effectively one delegated listener at the root rather than 1,000 individual ones.

nestedTopics.title: Root vs document
nestedTopics.explanation: React 16 delegated to document; React 17+ delegates to the root container, which helps when multiple React versions coexist on one page.

nestedTopics.title: Capture and bubble
nestedTopics.explanation: React supports both phases — e.g., onClickCapture runs during capture, onClick during bubble.

nestedTopics.title: stopPropagation scope
nestedTopics.explanation: Calling stopPropagation on a SyntheticEvent stops it from reaching parent React handlers, mirroring native bubbling within React's tree.

followUps.question: Why did React 17 move delegation from document to the root?
followUps.answer: So multiple independent React apps (or versions) on the same page do not interfere with each other's event handling and so stopPropagation at the document level behaves predictably.

followUps.question: How do you handle the capture phase?
followUps.answer: Use the Capture-suffixed props like onClickCapture or onFocusCapture.

scenario.question: A teammate writes onClick={handleDelete(item.id)} and the delete fires immediately on render for every row. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: handleDelete(item.id) CALLS the function during render and assigns its return value to onClick. You must pass a function instead: onClick={() => handleDelete(item.id)} so it runs only when clicked.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A classic mistake of invoking a handler in JSX instead of passing a reference, made worse when the handler needs an argument.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: JSX expressions are evaluated during render. Writing handleDelete(item.id) evaluates it right then; the event prop ends up holding whatever it returned (often undefined).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Wrapping it in an arrow function — () => handleDelete(item.id) — passes a function that React stores and only calls on the click, with the captured id.

scenario.whyImportant: Passing arguments to handlers comes up constantly with lists, and this off-by-parentheses bug is a frequent real-world and interview gotcha.

nestedTopics.title: Reference vs call
nestedTopics.explanation: onClick={fn} passes the function; onClick={fn()} calls it during render.

nestedTopics.title: Closures over arguments
nestedTopics.explanation: The arrow wrapper closes over item.id so each row gets its own id.

followUps.question: Is creating an arrow function per row a performance problem?
followUps.answer: Usually negligible. It only matters when children are memoized and rely on stable prop identity; then use useCallback or a data attribute read inside one shared handler.

coding.question: Build a controlled login form that prevents the default submit, shows the typed email, and clears on a reset button.
coding.thoughtProcess: I keep the email in state, drive the input with value + onChange, handle submit on the form with e.preventDefault(), and give Reset a type="button" so it does not submit. Derived display comes from the same state.
coding.lineByLine: useState('') holds the email. value + onChange make the input controlled. onSubmit calls e.preventDefault() so the page does not reload, then records the email. The Reset button uses type="button" so clicking it does not trigger form submission; it just clears state.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) per keystroke and per submit.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) in the length of the entered email.

alternativeApproaches.title: Uncontrolled with refs
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Read the value via a ref on submit instead of tracking every keystroke. Fewer re-renders, but you lose live derived values and the single source of truth.

followUps.question: Why set type="button" on Reset?
followUps.answer: Inside a form, a button defaults to type="submit", so without it Reset would submit the form too.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Keep handlers close to the state they update. For shared logic across many elements, use one handler and read identifying data from the event target (e.g., a data-id attribute) or pass the id via an arrow wrapper. Lift state up only when several components must react to the same event.
productionDeepDive.performance: React's delegation keeps listener counts low regardless of element count. The thing to watch is inline arrow functions creating new identities each render; this only hurts when passed to React.memo children. Stabilize with useCallback when profiling shows it matters — do not pre-optimize.
productionDeepDive.security: Treat all event-derived input as untrusted: validate and sanitize before storing or sending it. Never build HTML from raw input; avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user-controlled strings to prevent XSS.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As forms grow, centralize handling with a reducer (useReducer) or a form library (React Hook Form, Formik) instead of dozens of individual onChange handlers, which reduces boilerplate and re-renders.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Name handlers by intent (handleSubmit, handleSearchChange) and keep them small. Prefer one well-named shared handler over many near-duplicates.
productionDeepDive.observability: React DevTools and console logging in handlers help trace why and how often events fire; the Profiler shows whether handler-driven state changes cause excess re-renders.

caseStudies.problem: A large data grid attached a separate onClick to thousands of cells and felt sluggish to mount.
caseStudies.solution: Used a single delegated handler on the container that reads the clicked cell's data-id from the event target.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more logic in one handler vs far fewer closures and faster mounts.
caseStudies.lessons: Lean on event delegation for large collections instead of per-element handlers.

keyTakeaways: Event props are camelCased (onClick, onChange, onSubmit) and take a function reference, not a string or a function call.
React wraps native events in a cross-browser SyntheticEvent; event pooling existed before React 17 but was removed, so e.persist() is no longer needed.
React uses event delegation — a few listeners at the root, not one per element — which keeps large lists cheap.
Call e.preventDefault() to stop default behaviour (like form reloads) and e.stopPropagation() to stop bubbling to parent handlers.
To pass arguments, wrap the handler: onClick={() => handleClick(id)}; watch out for accidentally calling it during render.
